analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to pay pharmacies at least their cost to dispense drugs and standardizes pharmacy performance fees.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, which would have barred Medicare drug plans from paying pharmacies less than their cost to acquire and dispense drugs, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on June 20, 2023 and never received a committee vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require Medicare prescription drug plans to pay network pharmacies at least enough to cover each drug's acquisition and dispensing cost, after all discounts and back-end fees are netted out. It would give pharmacies a written appeal when a plan pays below their actual cost, force plans to disclose every pricing component of a claim, and require Medicare to evaluate and standardize the performance measures plans use to charge pharmacies fees. It was aimed at keeping community pharmacies — especially in rural areas — from being paid below cost and closing.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent, rural, and community pharmacies that are currently paid less than their cost to dispense Medicare drugs, and the patients — particularly in rural areas like Montana — who would lose access if those pharmacies close. Pharmacies gain a reimbursement floor, an appeal process through the Medicare ombudsman, disclosure of how each claim is priced, and protection from opaque or unreachable performance-based fees charged by plans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Community pharmacies and the patients they serve

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare drug plans to pay network pharmacies, net of all price concessions, discounts, and fees of any kind, at least enough to cover the pharmacy's cost to acquire and dispense each covered Part D drug.
Creates a written appeal process: a pharmacy paid below its lowest actual acquisition and dispensing cost can appeal to the Medicare Pharmaceutical and Technology Ombudsman within 60 days.

Directs Medicare to evaluate the performance measures plans use to charge pharmacies concessions and fees, examine whether targets are achievable, and establish standardized, evidence-based measures that plans must use for plan years starting in 2025.

Requires plans to promptly disclose to pharmacies all pricing components of each claim, including reimbursement identifiers, fees, concessions, and incentives, and defines 'specialty pharmacy' and affiliated entities to close loopholes.

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug plan sponsors (Part D insurers) and the pharmacy benefit managers that administer their networks, which currently recoup money from pharmacies through below-cost reimbursement rates, performance fees, and price concessions. Some of the added cost would flow through plan bids into Medicare Part D premiums and federal subsidies, meaning beneficiaries and taxpayers would bear part of the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare drug plans, PBMs, and premiums

drawbacks.text: Raising the reimbursement floor costs plans real money, and in Medicare Part D, higher plan costs flow into beneficiary premiums and federal subsidy payments, so beneficiaries and taxpayers would bear part of the price of the fix.

The bill mandates a heavy administrative build-out: Medicare must collect acquisition and dispensing cost surveys for every covered drug, set payment parameters drug by drug, and run a new appeals process, adding regulatory complexity to an already intricate payment system.

The most direct beneficiaries are pharmacy owners, a business interest; a supporter would have to acknowledge that better pharmacy margins and patient access mostly travel together here, but the bill does not directly cap what patients pay at the counter.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is real and modest in design: pharmacies that today accept below-cost reimbursement plus back-end fees because plans control network access would get a cost floor, transparency, and an appeal. The main cost is that higher payments to pharmacies raise plan expenses, some share of which lands on premiums and taxpayers, and the drug-by-drug payment parameters would be administratively demanding. On balance, for rural and independent pharmacies on the edge of closure, the benefits plausibly outweigh the costs — but the bill never got far enough for Congress to weigh them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee for the rest of the Congress; the committee never voted on it and the Senate never brought it to the floor.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Tester introduced the bill on June 20, 2023, joined by two Republican and one Democratic cosponsors (Capito, Lankford, and Brown).
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over Medicare.
No further action ever appears in the record: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare Part D insurers came out ahead: they keep the existing system in which pharmacies can be paid below cost and charged performance-based concessions, and rural patients who depend on independent pharmacies are left with the risk those pharmacies close.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug plans

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split evenly by party — one Democratic and two Republican cosponsors joined Tester — and no vote was ever recorded, so the bill never faced a partisan test on the floor.

industries.note: PBMs administer Medicare drug plan networks and make money by negotiating price concessions, performance fees, and reimbursement rates below pharmacies' cost. The bill would force payment up to pharmacies' actual cost, require claim-level pricing disclosure, and standardize the performance measures PBMs use to charge pharmacies — cutting off several of their revenue levers.

Plan sponsors would have to pay pharmacies a reimbursement floor net of all concessions, disclose every pricing component of a claim, and accept standardized performance measures. Their savings from squeezing pharmacies — some of which shows up in lower bids and premiums — would shrink.

Community, rural, and independent pharmacies would be guaranteed at least their cost to acquire and dispense each Medicare drug, gain an appeals process, and be protected from performance fees based on measures they cannot control. Their survival is directly tied to patients' access to a local pharmacy.
